profile.address: 9700, Cass Avenue, Lemont, DuPage County, Illinois, 60439
profile.reading:
This facility sits on the campus of Argonne National Laboratory at 9700 South Cass Avenue in Lemont, DuPage County, southwest of Chicago, and is managed by UChicago Argonne LLC, a company wholly owned by the University of Chicago that has held the operating contract for Argonne since the laboratory's founding in the 1940s as one of the first national laboratories established under the United States government's postwar atomic energy research program. Argonne is one of the U.S. Department of Energy's largest multi program national laboratories, conducting federally funded research across energy, physical sciences, biology, and computing.

The address matches Building 240 on the Argonne campus, home to the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility, a Department of Energy Office of Science user facility that gives researchers from universities, industry, and other government agencies access to some of the most powerful supercomputers in the world. Since January 2025, ALCF has operated Aurora, one of the first exascale computing systems ever built, capable of performing more than one quintillion calculations per second. Aurora is built from 10,624 compute nodes combining 21,248 Intel Xeon CPU Max Series processors with 63,744 Intel Data Center GPU Max Series accelerators, connected through a Slingshot 11 interconnect fabric, with 20.4 petabytes of aggregate system memory and 230 petabytes of high performance DAOS storage delivering up to 31 terabytes per second of throughput. Alongside Aurora, the facility also operates smaller systems including Polaris, Sophia, Crux, Tara, Minerva, and Janus, several of which serve as testbeds for artificial intelligence research.

Because Aurora and its supporting systems draw enormous amounts of electrical power and generate substantial heat, the building that houses them requires data center scale electrical infrastructure and cooling capacity engineered specifically for dense supercomputing hardware, though Argonne has not published a detailed public breakdown of the building's total power draw or cooling architecture. As a federally funded national laboratory facility rather than a commercial operation, this site exists to serve open scientific research under Department of Energy allocation programs, not paying customers, and it carries no commercial capacity, pricing, or leasing information because none applies. Its significance instead lies in its role as one of the country's primary hosts of exascale class computing infrastructure supporting climate modeling, materials science, drug discovery, and other large scale scientific computing programs that depend on Department of Energy supercomputing allocations.

reading.body:
Building 240 at Argonne National Laboratory in Lemont, southwest of Chicago, houses the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility, a Department of Energy Office of Science user facility that operates Aurora, an exascale supercomputer deployed in January 2025. Aurora comprises 10,624 compute nodes holding 21,248 Intel Xeon CPU Max Series processors and 63,744 Intel Data Center GPU Max Series accelerators connected through a Slingshot 11 fabric. The facility also operates several smaller systems, Polaris, Sophia, Crux, Tara, Minerva, and Janus, many serving as AI research testbeds. Argonne has not published the building's total electrical load or cooling specifications.

The power draw and cooling requirements of Aurora and its companion systems are engineering-scale, requiring data center grade electrical infrastructure and thermal management, but the operator has not disclosed megawatt figures or IT rack density. Without published power consumption, the campus cannot be ranked against other commercial facilities, though it serves Department of Energy scientific computing allocations rather than paying tenants and carries no commercial capacity or pricing.

This facility exists to host open scientific research in climate modeling, materials science, and drug discovery under Department of Energy supercomputing allocation programs, not commercial cloud or AI training services. Illinois has 44 mapped data center facilities, of which only six operators publish power figures totaling 236 megawatts. This campus ranks seventh in the state by published capacity, though its published capacity figure is not disclosed.
